I found relevant search results on off-grid solar design and New Mexico solar resources. Here are the key findings:

## New Mexico Solar Resources

New Mexico has peak sun hours of 5.5 – 6.5, which is excellent for solar installations and comparable to the Navajo Nation area (which spans Arizona, Utah, and New Mexico). Average solar irradiance in the Navajo Nation area is 5.5 – 6.5 kWh/m²/day.

## Off-Grid Design for Winter Worst Month

For off-grid systems in general, off grid systems are most concerned with optimizing tilt angle to achieve the highest minimum irradiation value during the critical design month, which refers to the month with the lowest available radiation levels and subsequently the longest nights. December would be the critical design month for someplace like New York State, which has a latitude of about 45 degrees north.

## Tilt Angle with Latitude +15°

For off-grid systems, a fixed tilt of latitude + 15° is recommended for winter bias. This approach optimizes panel orientation to capture maximum solar energy during the critical winter months when solar production is lowest.

Your worst month matters more than your average—if you're designing for true off-grid living, you need to handle January, not just August.

content.text:
## Framing the problem

Off-grid sizing isn't "annual average production ≥ annual average load" — it's "worst-case day production + battery buffer ≥ load, every single day of the year, including December." Two numbers drive everything: the **design-month sun hours** (not the annual average) and the **total system loss chain** from panel-rated watts to usable electrons at the outlet.

## Step 1 — Solar resource at 35°N high desert NM

NREL PVWatts data for Albuquerque show December (the worst month) delivers only **~4.4 peak sun hours (PSH)** at a shallow 20° tilt — well below the ~5.5–6.5 PSH annual-average figure often quoted for New Mexico. That gap is the whole reason sizing on the annual average is a trap for a year-round cabin.

Off-grid convention is to tilt the array steeper than latitude — **latitude + 15° (~50° here)** — to favor low winter sun angles at the cost of some summer overproduction (which you don't need anyway). That steeper tilt recovers some of the December deficit; a reasonable, still-conservative design value is:

**Design-month PSH ≈ 4.5 hours/day**

## Step 2 — Loss chain (panel-rated W → usable Wh)

| Loss | Typical factor |
|---|---|
| Soiling/dust (desert) | ~0.95 |
| Temperature/mismatch/wiring | ~0.95 |
| MPPT charge controller | ~0.97 |
| LiFePO4 round-trip efficiency | ~0.96 |
| Inverter (AC loads) | ~0.93 |
| **Combined** | **≈ 0.75–0.80** |

This is the standard "derate factor" used in off-grid design — I'll use **0.77**.

## Step 3 — Array size

$$\text{Array (W)} = \frac{\text{Load (Wh/day)}}{\text{PSH} \times \text{derate}} = \frac{1500}{4.5 \times 0.77} \approx 433\,\text{W}$$

Add margin for panel degradation (~0.5%/yr), occasional snow cover, and consecutive cloudy days (20–25%):

$$433 \times 1.25 \approx 540\,\text{W}$$

**→ Array: ~500–600 W STC**, mounted at ~45–50° tilt, true south. In practice I'd round up to a standard module combination — e.g., two 300 W panels or a single 550–600 W panel — rather than chase the exact number, since panel cost is the cheapest part of the system and headroom buys resilience against runs of bad weather.

## Step 4 — Battery bank (3 days autonomy)

$$\text{Usable energy needed} = 1.5\,\text{kWh/day} \times 3\,\text{days} = 4.5\,\text{kWh}$$

LiFePO4 tolerates deep cycling well, but for cycle-life longevity you still design to **~80% DoD**, not 100%, even though the chemistry can technically go deeper:

$$\text{Nameplate capacity} = \frac{4.5\,\text{kWh}}{0.80} \approx 5.6\,\text{kWh}$$

**→ Battery bank: ~5.5–6 kWh nameplate** (e.g., a 48 V 120 Ah pack ≈ 5.76 kWh, or two 51.2 V 100 Ah packs in parallel ≈ 10.2 kWh if you want extra margin/future load growth).

## Summary

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| Design-month PSH (35°N, lat+15° tilt) | ~4.5 h/day |
| System derate | ~0.77 |
| **PV array** | **~500–600 W** |
| DoD target (LiFePO4) | 80% |
| **Battery bank** | **~5.5–6 kWh nameplate** |

Two caveats worth flagging explicitly: (1) this assumes 1.5 kWh/day is the *true* load including any inverter standby/parasitic draw — that idle draw (often 10–20 W continuous) is a classic underestimate and quietly adds 0.25–0.5 kWh/day; verify it's already in your number. (2) The array is sized to cover a *typical* design-month day, not to fully recharge the battery the day after a 3-day autonomy event in bad weather — if back-to-back cloudy stretches are a real risk at your site, bias upward toward 700–800 W rather than the bare-minimum 500 W.

Sources:
- [New Mexico peak sun hours](https://www.thegreenwatt.com/new-mexico-peak-sun-hours/)
- [Solar in Albuquerque, NM: 2026 Cost, Savings & Payback](https://jouleio.com/solar/albuquerque-nm/)
- [Driven Design of a Stand-Alone PV System to Support Residential Loads on the Navajo Nation](https://www.nmlegis.gov/(X(1)S(0d3dh1cyocbnztybqvja2dch))/handouts/STTC%20062326%20Item%205%20Driven%20Design%20of%20a%20Stand-Alone%20PV%20System%20to%20Support%20Residential%20Loads%20on%20the%20Navajo%20Nation.pdf)
- [Complete Off-Grid Solar System Design Guide](https://muhammed.portlandiaelectric.supply/blogs/energy-solutions/complete-off-grid-solar-system-design-guide)
